hints: The tricky symbol is *: it always belongs to the character just before it. So when you look at a pattern position, first check whether the next pattern character is a star.
DP on suffixes: dp[i][j] = does t[i..] match p[j..]? A x* pair either matches nothing (skip the pair) or eats one matching character and stays on the same pair.

1. dp[n][m] = true (both empty). Fill i from n down to 0 and j from m-1 down to 0.
  2. first = i < n and (p[j] == t[i] or p[j] == '.').
  3. If p[j+1] == '*': dp[i][j] = dp[i][j+2] || (first && dp[i+1][j]).
  4. Otherwise: dp[i][j] = first && dp[i+1][j+1].
  5. Return dp[0][0].

approaches.name: Plain recursion
approaches.idea: Try both star choices (skip / consume) recursively without remembering results; blows up on inputs like many a*.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Bottom-up DP over (text position, pattern position).

explain: For t = "xxyz", p = "x*y.": the pair x* can eat both xs (consume twice, staying on the pair), then skip itself; y matches y, and . matches z, reaching the end of both → true. The invariant: dp[i][j] only uses cells with larger i or larger j, which are already filled. Edge case: an empty text can still match a pattern like "z*", because the star pair may match zero characters — that's why i runs all the way to n.
recognize: Pattern with '.' (any char) and '*' (repeat previous) matched against the whole text → 2D DP on (text index, pattern index).
